content: Jaundice is characterized by a yellowish discoloration of the skin, the conjunctiva (the clear covering over the sclera or whites of the eyes), and mucous membranes. This discoloration is caused by hyperbilirubinemia, which refers to elevated levels of bilirubin in the blood. For jaundice to become visibly apparent, the bilirubin concentration in the blood typically needs to exceed 2–3 mg/dL. The term jaundice originates from the French word jaune, meaning yellow. Historically, it was mistakenly believed that individuals with jaundice perceived everything as yellow, but this is not true. In 1885, Luhrman identified jaundice as a potential adverse effect of vaccination. In 1935, the American surgeon A.O. Whipple first described obstructive jaundice. Between 1950 and 2000, many viruses responsible for hepatitis and jaundice were discovered. Jaundice is classified into two main categories: unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia can result from increased bilirubin production, reduced hepatic uptake, or defects in bilirubin conjugation. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, on the other hand, is further subdivided into causes such as biliary tract obstruction, intrahepatic cholestasis, hepatocellular parenchymal injury, and defects in hepatocellular canalicular excretion or re-uptake in sinusoids. Bilirubin is a byproduct of heme catabolism, which occurs primarily in the liver and spleen. It undergoes several metabolic processes, including hepatic uptake, conjugation, clearance, and excretion into bile. Jaundice develops when bilirubin levels increase and deposit under the skin, leading to the characteristic yellow discoloration. Neonatal jaundice can arise from physiological bilirubin accumulation or pathological mechanisms. Pathological neonatal jaundice may be acquired or inherited. Acquired causes include Rh hemolytic disease, ABO incompatibility, and hemolytic disease due to G6PD enzyme deficiency. Inherited causes involve defects in bilirubin metabolism, such as Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome types I and II, Lucey-Driscoll syndrome, Dubin-Johnson syndrome, and Rotor syndrome. The causes of jaundice are categorized based on whether they result in conjugated or unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia arises from increased bilirubin production, impaired hepatic uptake, or defective conjugation, leading to an accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is often due to intrahepatic or extrahepatic cholestasis, which causes conjugated bilirubin to accumulate. Jaundice is a clinical sign of hyperbilirubinemia, with visible yellowing of the skin, conjunctiva, and mucous membranes when bilirubin levels exceed 2–3 mg/dL. The incidence of jaundice is approximately 40,000 per 100,000 individuals in intensive care unit patients. Neonatal jaundice is more common in Asian and mixed Asian/White infants compared to White infants. Hepatocellular jaundice, often caused by viral hepatitis, typically affects younger patients, while cholestatic jaundice, associated with liver cancer, hepatitis, and cirrhosis, is more common in older patients. Males are more frequently affected by hepatocellular jaundice and liver cancer, whereas females are more commonly affected by hemolytic jaundice, particularly from cholangiocarcinoma. Risk factors for jaundice are also classified based on conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Common risk factors for unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia include the neonatal period, certain drugs (e.g., rifampin, probenecid), syndromes like Gilbert's and Crigler-Najjar types I and II, steroids, and chronic liver diseases. Risk factors for conjugated hyperbilirubinemia include viral hepatitis, alcohol, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, chronic hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, drugs and toxins (e.g., alkylated steroids, chlorpromazine, herbal medications, arsenic), sepsis, hypoperfusion states, infiltrative diseases (e.g., amyloidosis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis), pregnancy, cirrhosis, choledocholithiasis, intrinsic and extrinsic biliary tract tumors, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and acute or chronic pancreatitis. Routine screening for jaundice is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. The natural history of jaundice varies widely, with symptoms manifesting at any age depending on the underlying cause. The severity and type of complications also depend on the etiology. Some individuals may recover fully without long-term complications, while for others, jaundice may signal a life-threatening condition. The gold standard diagnostic test for jaundice is measuring plasma bilirubin levels. A bilirubin concentration exceeding 2–3 mg/dL is typically required for visible discoloration. Patients with jaundice may report symptoms such as yellowing of the skin, nausea, vomiting, fever, anorexia, dark urine, fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant pain. A detailed history of alcohol use, blood transfusions, viral hepatitis, and family history of liver disease is essential. Physical examination findings in jaundice include yellowish discoloration of the skin and sclerae, which indicate elevated serum bilirubin levels. Additional findings may include cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and peripheral edema. Laboratory findings reveal elevated serum total bilirubin levels, which can be categorized as conjugated or unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Imaging studies such as abdominal CT scans, MRI, and ultrasonography can aid in diagnosing underlying causes like cirrhosis. CT and MRI findings suggestive of cirrhosis include liver shrinkage and atrophy, dilated portal or splanchnic veins, esophageal varices, collateral vessels, splenomegaly, and ascites. Ultrasonography may reveal pathognomonic findings such as recanalization of the umbilical vein, indicative of portal hypertension. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is another imaging modality for diagnosing cholestasis. Liver biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing jaundice caused by cirrhosis, though it is rarely necessary. Biopsy samples can be obtained via percutaneous, transjugular, or laparoscopic approaches. However, liver biopsy carries risks, particularly in patients with cirrhosis, and is generally avoided if clinical, laboratory, and radiologic data strongly suggest cirrhosis. Treatment of jaundice focuses on addressing the underlying cause, such as viral hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, or cirrhosis. Medical therapy aims to conjugate unconjugated bilirubin or enhance bilirubin clearance and excretion. Surgery is not a first-line treatment for jaundice but may be necessary in cases of cirrhosis, cholestasis, or liver failure. Surgical options include transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting (TIPS), cholecystectomy, and liver transplantation.
